title: Key Organs in Metabolic Integration
objectives: Identify the metabolic roles of major organs
Explain organ-specific fuel preferences and pathways
Analyze clinical consequences of organ dysfunction

liver.title: Liver: The Metabolic Supervisor
liver.content:
Hepatic Metabolic Functions

1. Carbohydrate Metabolism

  • Fed state: Glycogenesis, glycolysis
  • Fasted state: Glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis
  • Maintains blood glucose (4-6 mM)

2. Lipid Metabolism

  • Synthesis: Fatty acids, TAG, cholesterol
  • Export: VLDL to peripheral tissues
  • Ketogenesis during prolonged fasting

3. Detoxification

  • Ammonia → urea (urea cycle)
  • Drug metabolism (CYP450)
  • Bilirubin conjugation

Clinical Correlation: Liver Failure

  • Hypoglycemia: Impaired gluconeogenesis
  • Hyperammonemia: Urea cycle dysfunction
  • Jaundice: Bilirubin processing failure

muscle.title: Muscle: Energy Consumer
muscle.content:
Muscle Metabolic Specialization

1. Fuel Utilization

  • Resting: Fatty acid oxidation
  • Exercise: Glycogenolysis → lactate (anaerobic) or pyruvate oxidation (aerobic)
  • Creatine phosphate buffer for rapid ATP

2. Protein Metabolism

  • Major reservoir of amino acids
  • Releases alanine (glucose-alanine cycle)

Clinical Correlation: McArdle Disease

  • Glycogen phosphorylase deficiency
  • Exercise intolerance + myoglobinuria
  • Treatment: High-protein diet (FA oxidation)

adipose.title: Adipose Tissue: Energy Bank
adipose.content:
Adipocyte Functions

1. Lipid Storage & Release

  • Fed state: LPL-mediated TAG uptake
  • Fasted state: HSL-mediated lipolysis → FFAs
  • Leptin secretion (satiety signal)

2. Endocrine Role

  • Adiponectin (insulin sensitizer)
  • Resistin (insulin resistance)

Clinical Correlation: Lipodystrophy

  • Loss of fat → ectopic lipid deposition
  • Severe insulin resistance
  • Leptin replacement therapy

brain.title: Brain: Metabolic Priority
brain.content:
Neuronal Energy Demands

1. Fuel Preferences

  • Normal: Glucose (GLUT1/3 transporters)
  • Starvation: Ketones (after 3-5 days)
  • No glycogen stores → constant supply needed

2. Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB)

  • Selective permeability (excludes FFAs)
  • Kernicterus risk (unconjugated bilirubin)

Clinical Correlation: Hypoglycemia

  • Neuroglycopenia → confusion, seizures
  • No ketone adaptation (acute setting)
  • Emergency treatment: IV dextrose

kidney.title: Kidney: Metabolic Partner
kidney.content:
Renal Metabolic Roles

1. Gluconeogenesis

  • Produces 25% of glucose during fasting
  • Uses glutamine (from muscle)

2. Acid-Base Balance

  • Excretes NH4+ (from glutaminase)
  • Reclaims HCO3-

Clinical Correlation: Renal Failure

  • Metabolic acidosis (↓NH4+ excretion)
  • Hyperphosphatemia/hypocalcemia
  • Uremia → anorexia/catabolism

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
FAQs

Q: Why can't the liver use ketones for energy? +

A: Liver lacks mitochondrial succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid-CoA transferase (SCOT), the enzyme required to activate ketones. It exports ketones for other tissues (brain/heart).

Q: How does muscle protect the brain during fasting? +

A: Muscle switches to fatty acid oxidation, sparing glucose for the brain. It also exports gluconeogenic precursors (alanine/lactate) to the liver.

Q: Why does adipose tissue dysfunction cause diabetes? +

A> Dysregulated lipolysis floods the liver with FFAs → ↑gluconeogenesis + ↓insulin signaling. Loss of adiponectin exacerbates insulin resistance.
